form.label: MITRE ATT&CK
form.description: Which adversary techniques the fleet's open vulnerabilities could enable.

search.query: | `riskability_host_platforms($host_tok|s$)` | eval host_plat_re = if(isnull(rk_fams) OR mvcount(mvfilter(rk_fams=="__unknown__"))>0, "Windows|Linux|macOS", mvjoin(rk_fams, "|")) | eval host_plat_label = if(host_plat_re=="Windows|Linux|macOS", "all platforms", mvjoin(rk_fams, ", ")) | table host_plat_re, host_plat_label

div.b: This page shows exposure, not attack evidence.
div.span:
CVE → CWE → CAPEC → ATT&CK technique is a published MITRE mapping: many-to-many and lossy. It says this weakness class is the kind of thing that enables that technique, not that anyone used it or that the CVE is exploitable here. A CVE with no CWE, or an unmapped CWE, never appears - absence is not safety. For real-world exploitation rather than classification, see KEV and EPSS on Findings.
This page can only ever speak about a quarter of ATT&CK. Enterprise ATT&CK currently holds 697 live techniques and sub-techniques. CAPEC is the narrow hop: only 177 of its 559 attack patterns carry an ATT&CK mapping at all, and between them they name just 179 techniques. Twelve of those come from a CAPEC with no weakness attached, leaving 167 this app can reach. The other 530 are not techniques your fleet is safe from. They are techniques this chain has nothing to say about, because MITRE never mapped them, and no amount of scanning will make them appear.
The Confidence filter gates every panel on this page, and it defaults to High only. Confidence is how sure the matcher is that the package is genuinely the product an advisory names. It is about identity, not severity. A Linux package installed by a package manager carries an exact identity, so its matches are high confidence. Windows software is identified from a display name, so every Windows finding is low confidence by construction, leads to verify rather than facts. At the default setting this page is therefore mostly the Linux fleet, and a known-exploited finding on a Windows host sits behind the filter. Panels say so when they are hiding something; set Confidence to All to see everything.

search.query: | `riskability_kev_bridge_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)`

| `riskability_kev_bridge_for($host_tok|s$, "*")` | stats dc(cve_id) AS rk_all, dc(eval(if($conf_tok|s$="*" OR confidence=$conf_tok|s$, cve_id, null()))) AS rk_shown | eval rk_hidden = rk_all - rk_shown

div.b: $kev_conf_hidden$ known-exploited mapped finding(s) sit below your confidence filter.
div.span: These are CVEs on the CISA KEV list that MITRE has mapped to a technique, but the match on this fleet is lower confidence than the filter allows, so they are not drawn above. A lower confidence match can be a false positive, which is why the filter is honoured, but known-exploited is the one category worth a second look: set Confidence to All to see them.

search.query: stats dc(cve_id) AS value, values(comment) AS comment BY tech_label, reach_class | eval tier = case(reach_class="answers any address","act-now", reach_class="answers one address","act-soon", reach_class="loopback only","plan", reach_class="no listening port","watch", 1=1,"unknown-risk") | eval comment = mvindex(comment, 0) | table tech_label, reach_class, value, tier, comment

viz.option: No known-exploited CVE in this scope maps to a technique in MITRE's KEV mapping. That is not a clean bill of health: it means none of your KEV findings are among the ones CTID has mapped so far.

div.b: This panel is a floor, not a full picture.
div.span: It shows only known-exploited CVEs that MITRE's Center for Threat-Informed Defense has mapped to a technique. That mapping covers a subset of the KEV catalogue, so a known-exploited CVE with no row here is unmapped, not safe. The colour is the reach of the finding, not how many there are: one known-exploited package answering the network is drawn as loud as a thousand that answer nothing, because reachable is the thing this page adds to what EPSS and KEV already tell you. Unlike the matrix below, this is not a weakness-class inference: CISA recorded these CVEs being exploited, and MITRE mapped each to the technique that does it. A row marked (impact) is the technique the CVE achieves after exploitation, and (ransomware flag) is a campaign level marker CISA sets rather than a mapping of this CVE, so it is the weakest claim here and is labelled as such.

panel.title: Configuration surface: techniques the host is measured to run

search.query: | inputlookup riskability_config_lookup | search hostname=$host_tok|s$ | stats count AS mechanisms, sum(n_evidence) AS weaknesses, dc(hostname) AS hosts BY attack, kind | eval label = attack . " " . case(kind="cron", "cron jobs", kind="systemd-timer", "systemd timers", kind="systemd-service", "systemd services", kind="suid", "SUID and SGID binaries", kind="scheduled-task", "Scheduled Tasks", kind="autorun", "Run key and Startup autoruns", 1=1, kind) | eval series = if(weaknesses > 0, "flagged by swinv", "surface, no weakness flagged") | sort 50000 - mechanisms | table label, series, mechanisms

viz.option: No configuration records. Either the collector is not running with the config include flag, or this bundle predates config support. Absence here is missing data, not a hardened host.

div.b: Measured configuration, counted in mechanisms, not a vulnerability finding.
div.span: Each bar is a persistence or privilege mechanism the collector read directly from the host, and the ATT&CK technique it is the surface for. Six mechanisms are collected: cron, systemd timers, systemd services and SUID binaries on Linux, Scheduled Tasks and Run key autoruns on Windows. The techniques behind them are exactly the kind a CVE feed can never reach, which is why they appear nowhere in the matrix below. A mechanism is not itself a weakness: a root cron job whose script anyone can write, or a SUID binary no package owns, is the finding, and swinv makes that judgment because it knows the context an outside join does not. The weaknesses count is swinv's, carried through untouched. On a clean host it is zero, and the bar is the surface an attacker would look at, not a list of problems.

search.query: | inputlookup riskability_config_lookup | search hostname=$host_tok|s$ | eval label = attack . " " . case(kind="cron", "cron jobs", kind="systemd-timer", "systemd timers", kind="systemd-service", "systemd services", kind="suid", "SUID and SGID binaries", kind="scheduled-task", "Scheduled Tasks", kind="autorun", "Run key and Startup autoruns", 1=1, kind) | search label=$cfg_label_tok|s$ | eval owner = if(isnull(purl) OR purl="", "no package owns this", replace(replace(purl, "^pkg:[^/]+/", ""), "\?.*$", "")) | eval flagged = if(tonumber(n_evidence) > 0, n_evidence, "none") | eval writable = case(world_writable="true" OR world_writable=1, "anyone can write it", isnull(world_writable) OR world_writable="", "", 1=1, "no") | sort 50000 hostname, name | table hostname, name, path, user, schedule, owner, mode, writable, flagged | rename hostname AS "Host", name AS "Name", path AS "Path", user AS "Runs as", schedule AS "Schedule", owner AS "Owning package", mode AS "Mode", writable AS "World writable", flagged AS "Weaknesses flagged"

viz.option: Nothing behind this bar at the current host filter. Changing the host after clicking can leave this pointing at a bar that no longer exists; click the chart again.

div.span: Each row is something the host is configured to run, read directly from disk. Owning package says which package put it there, and no package owns this is the interesting case rather than the alarming one: it is often a container or a snap, which is why the collector's own weakness count, not this column, decides what is a finding. Weaknesses flagged is that count, and none is the ordinary state of a healthy host. World writable is the one that turns a mechanism into a route on its own: a scheduled job running as root whose script anyone on the box can rewrite is that job running as anyone. It is blank where the collector does not report it, which on Windows is everywhere.

search.query: search tech_label=$kev_tech_tok|s$ reach_class=$kev_reach_tok|s$ | stats values(title) AS title, values(reach_class) AS reach, values(comment) AS how, values(map_strength) AS strength, values(confidence) AS confidence BY cve_id, hostname, package | eval title = mvindex(title, 0), how = mvindex(how, 0), strength = mvindex(strength, 0) | eval strength = case(strength="recorded", "recorded exploitation", strength="recorded-impact", "recorded impact", strength="implied", "implied by ransomware flag", 1=1, strength) | table cve_id, title, hostname, package, confidence, reach, strength, how | rename cve_id AS "CVE", title AS "What it is", hostname AS "Host", package AS "Package", confidence AS "Confidence", reach AS "Reachable here", strength AS "Claim", how AS "What MITRE recorded"

viz.option: Nothing behind this cell at the current filters. Changing Host or Confidence after drilling can leave this pointing at a cell that no longer exists; click the chart again.

panel.title: ATT&CK matrix - where open findings sit in an attack

search.query: | inputlookup riskability_techstate_lookup | eval rk_gate = "$matrix_fleet_q$" | eval rk_want = if("$src_tok$" = "*", "any", "$src_tok$") | where map_source = rk_want | search confidence=$conf_tok|s$ | stats sum(cves) AS cves, values(platforms) AS rk_pf BY tactic_name, tactic_order, technique_name, technique | eval rk_has_hostos = if(match(rk_pf, "(?i)Windows|Linux|macOS"), 1, 0) | eval rk_in_scope = if(match(rk_pf, "(?i)($host_plat_re$)"), 1, 0) | where rk_has_hostos = 0 OR rk_in_scope = 1

| `riskability_attack_matrix_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)` | eval rk_gate = "$matrix_host_q$" | search map_source=$src_tok|s$ | stats dc(cve_id) AS cves, values(platforms) AS rk_pf BY tactic_name, tactic_order, technique_name, technique | eval rk_has_hostos = if(match(rk_pf, "(?i)Windows|Linux|macOS"), 1, 0) | eval rk_in_scope = if(match(rk_pf, "(?i)($host_plat_re$)"), 1, 0) | where rk_has_hostos = 0 OR rk_in_scope = 1

eventstats max(cves) AS peak BY technique_name | sort 50000 - peak | streamstats dc(technique_name) AS rk_rank | where rk_rank <= 120 | sort 50000 tactic_order | fields tactic_name, technique_name, cves

viz.option: No tactic data. Either the rollup has not run yet (it runs hourly at :43) or the bundle lacks the ATT&CK tactic mapping - rebuild with --mitre and import.

search.query: eventstats max(cves) AS peak BY technique_name | sort 50000 - peak | streamstats dc(technique_name) AS rk_rank | where rk_rank <= 120 | sort 50000 tactic_order | fields tactic_name, technique_name, cves

viz.option: No tactic data. The ATT&CK tactic mapping is missing from the bundle, not the exposure - rebuild with --mitre and import.

search.query: stats dc(technique_name) AS rk_total | eval rk_hidden = if(rk_total > 120, rk_total - 120, 0) | table rk_total, rk_hidden

div.b: This matrix is not showing everything. $matrix_hidden$ of $matrix_total$ techniques are hidden.
div.span: The grid draws the 120 techniques carrying the most distinct CVEs, because more than that cannot be read at this size. The rest are not absent and not safe, they are off the picture. The table below is not capped this way, so filter to a host or pick a tactic to reach them, and read this grid as the shape of the fleet rather than an inventory of it.

search.query: | inputlookup riskability_attack_ledger_lookup | search confidence=$conf_tok|s$ | stats sum(total_open_cves) AS t, sum(placed_any) AS p, sum(via_chain) AS c, sum(only_inherited) AS i, sum(only_vector) AS v, sum(only_observed) AS o, sum(no_cwe_at_all) AS n, sum(unplaced) AS u

div.b: $lg_t$ unique open CVEs in scope. $lg_p$ can be placed on ATT&CK. $lg_u$ cannot, and unplaced is not not-vulnerable.
div.span: Of the placed: $lg_c$ through the asserted chain, where MITRE maps the CVE's own weakness class to attack patterns; $lg_i$ more only by inheritance from a parent weakness class, one or two steps up and never from a top level category; $lg_v$ more only by inference from the CVSS vector, which needs no weakness class at all; and $lg_o$ only because the vulnerable package is observed answering the network. Each is a different strength of claim, the Mapping evidence filter isolates any of them, and they are never added into one number. Of the unplaced, $lg_n$ carry no weakness class and no mappable vector, which is a gap in the record, not a clean bill. These counts are unique CVEs, not findings, because counting per host would inflate the taxonomy by the size of the fleet.

div.b: An empty matrix means the tactic mapping is missing.
div.span: The grid needs MITRE's technique-to-tactic mapping, carried only by bundles a recent feed builder built with --mitre: rebuild and import. Without tactics the technique list below is still correct, just not placeable in an attack sequence. Cells count distinct CVEs; a technique appears under every tactic MITRE assigns it, so a row counts the same CVEs more than once.

A technique that can only run on an operating system this scope does not include is dropped, because the chain says it "could enable" a technique that cannot execute here, which is a void claim rather than a faint one. Techniques that name no host operating system, such as reconnaissance and cloud techniques, are always kept: an absent row there would be a gap in the mapping, not a clean host. Platform is matched on the host, never on the CVE. On a fleet wide view every platform present is in scope, so nothing is dropped for platform alone.

panel.title: Techniques enabled by open findings, most exposed first

search.query: | `riskability_attack_surface_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)` | stats dc(cve_id) AS cves, dc(hostname) AS hosts, dc(package) AS packages, values(cwe) AS weaknesses, max(epss) AS peak_epss, values(platforms) AS rk_pf BY technique, technique_name | eval rk_has_hostos = if(match(rk_pf, "(?i)Windows|Linux|macOS"), 1, 0) | eval rk_in_scope = if(match(rk_pf, "(?i)($host_plat_re$)"), 1, 0) | where rk_has_hostos = 0 OR rk_in_scope = 1 | eval platforms = if(rk_pf="", "any (no host OS named)", mvjoin(rk_pf, ", ")) | eval peak_epss = round(peak_epss, 4) | sort 50000 - cves | table technique, technique_name, cves, hosts, packages, weaknesses, peak_epss, platforms | rename technique AS "Technique", technique_name AS "Name", cves AS "CVEs", hosts AS "Hosts", packages AS "Packages", weaknesses AS "Via CWE", peak_epss AS "Peak EPSS", platforms AS "Runs on"

viz.option: No open finding maps to a technique. Most CVEs carry no CWE: usually a mapping gap, not an absence of exposure.

div.b: Ordered by how many CVEs, not by whether they can be reached.
div.span: The rank is the count of distinct open CVEs mapping to each technique, so a technique sits at the top on volume alone even when nothing behind it answers the network. For reach, read the known-exploited panel above and the CAPEC table below. A CVE that enables several techniques is counted under each, so the CVEs column does not sum to a fleet total. Platform filtered like the matrix: a technique that can only run on an operating system this scope does not include is dropped.

panel.title: Weakness classes present in the fleet (CWE)

search.query: | `riskability_finding_cwes_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)` | stats dc(cve_id) AS cves BY cwe | sort 50000 - cves | head 40

viz.option: No open finding carries a CWE. Most CVEs have no recorded weakness class: a mapping gap, not an absence of risk. See the coverage panel.

div.b: Area is CVEs carrying the weakness, not severity.
div.span: The treemap draws the 40 largest weakness classes, sized by how many open CVEs carry each. A CVE mapped to several CWEs is counted under each, so the tiles do not add up to your CVE total, and a big tile means a common weakness rather than a severe one.

search.query: | `riskability_open_findings_for($host_tok|s$)` | lookup riskability_advisory_lookup cve_id OUTPUT cwes | eval mapped = case(isnull(cwes) OR cwes=="", "no CWE recorded for this CVE", 1=1, "has a CWE") | stats dc(cve_id) AS cves BY mapped | eventstats sum(cves) AS total | eval share = round(cves*100/total, 1)."%" | fields mapped, cves, share | rename mapped AS "Mapping status", cves AS "CVEs", share AS "Share"

div.b: The "no CWE recorded" row is this page's blind spot, not a footnote.
div.span: Every panel here starts from a CVE's weakness class, so a finding with no CWE cannot appear on any of them, however exploitable it is. Read that share as the fraction of your open findings this dashboard cannot place, not as a data quality detail. This count covers all open findings in the host scope at every confidence, so the Confidence filter does not change it.

panel.title: Which weaknesses lead to which techniques - $tech_label$

search.query: | `riskability_attack_surface_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)` | search $tech_filter$ $cwe_filter$ | stats dc(cve_id) AS cves BY cwe, technique_name | sort 50000 - cves | head 25

viz.option: No open finding has a CWE that MITRE links to a technique.

div.span: One weakness can enable several techniques, so a CVE is drawn once per technique it reaches. Each ribbon is correct alone (that many distinct CVEs link that CWE to that technique), but totals double-count. Read concentration, not totals. Top 25 links only.

search.query: | `riskability_attack_surface_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)` | search $tech_filter$ $cwe_filter$ | stats min(epss) AS lo, perc25(epss) AS q1, median(epss) AS med, perc75(epss) AS q3, max(epss) AS hi, dc(cve_id) AS cves BY technique_name | where cves >= 3 | sort 50000 - cves | head 15 | fields technique_name, lo, q1, med, q3, hi

viz.option: Not enough scored CVEs per technique to plot a distribution. EPSS comes from the feed; without it in the bundle there is nothing to plot.

div.b: Boxes show the EPSS spread per technique, not its peak.
div.span: The table above reports each technique's highest EPSS, which one CVE can dominate; a box separates many likely-exploited CVEs from a single outlier. Techniques with fewer than three scored CVEs are omitted.
Click a technique, matrix cell, CWE tile, Sankey ribbon or box below to narrow this page to it.
Page narrowed. The panels below show only what matches; the matrix and technique list stay whole so you can pick something else.
Filtered by $drill_note$

These findings are real vulnerabilities. The technique is what MITRE says this weakness class could enable, not something anyone observed, and it is two steps removed from the CVE: the advisory names a weakness class, and that class maps to techniques. A technique can therefore read oddly for a particular CVE. Read the "What it is" column first and treat the technique as the category, not the finding. Read the technique on attack.mitre.org (needs internet).

search.query: | `riskability_attack_surface_detail_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)` | search $tech_filter$ $cwe_filter$ | eval root = if(scope_id!="", scope_id, "host") | eval installed_version = last_version | table cve_id, title, severity, epss, package, installed_version, fixed_version, hostname, root, technique, technique_name, cwe, via_capec | sort 50000 technique, - epss | rename cve_id AS "CVE", title AS "What it is", severity AS "Severity", epss AS "EPSS", package AS "Package", installed_version AS "Installed", fixed_version AS "Fixed in", hostname AS "Host", root AS "Root", technique AS "Technique", technique_name AS "Technique name", cwe AS "CWE", via_capec AS "Via CAPEC"

viz.option: No findings map to a technique at this confidence filter.

panel.title: One control, many techniques: mitigations ranked by reachable coverage

search.query: | `riskability_mitigation_coverage_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)` | eventstats sum(techniques) AS rk_total BY mitigation | sort 50000 - rk_total | streamstats dc(mitigation) AS rk_rank | where rk_rank <= 15 | eval category = mitigation . " " . mitigation_name, series = reach_class, value = techniques | table category, series, value

viz.option: No reachable finding maps to a technique with a MITRE mitigation. With no inventory or no mapping, that is silence rather than a clean fleet.

div.b: The bar is techniques covered, coloured by reach.
div.span: Each mitigation is ranked by how many distinct ATT&CK techniques it would address among the fleet's open findings, and the segments split that by whether the finding answers the network. A control with a long "answers any address" segment is the one to reach for first. This is coverage of the mapped and reachable set, not a promise: a mitigation reduces the technique, it does not patch the CVE, and the CVEs still need fixing. Techniques with no MITRE mitigation are not counted here, so this is a floor.

search.query: | `riskability_mitigation_rows_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)` | eval category = mitigation . " " . mitigation_name | search category=$mit_label_tok|s$ | eval rk_rank = case(reach_class="answers any address", 0, reach_class="answers one address", 1, reach_class="loopback only", 2, reach_class="no listening port", 3, 1=1, 4) | stats dc(cve_id) AS cves, min(rk_rank) AS rk_rank, values(description) AS how BY technique, technique_name | eval how = mvindex(how, 0) | eval how = replace(how, "\(Citation:[^)]*\)", "") | eval how = trim(replace(how, "\s+", " ")) | eval how = if(len(how) > 240, substr(how, 1, 237) . "...", how) | eval reach = case(rk_rank=0, "answers any address", rk_rank=1, "answers one address", rk_rank=2, "loopback only", rk_rank=3, "no listening port", 1=1, "not assessed") | sort 50000 rk_rank, - cves | table technique, technique_name, reach, cves, how | rename technique AS "Technique", technique_name AS "What it is", reach AS "Most reachable finding behind it", cves AS "Open CVEs behind it", how AS "What this control does about it"

viz.option: Nothing behind this bar at the current filters. Changing Host or Confidence after clicking can leave this pointing at a control that no longer appears; click the chart again.

div.b: Coverage, split by how reachable the findings behind it are.
div.span: The rows that answer the network are the ones this control earns its place on. A control that covers many techniques which nothing can reach is still worth having, but it is not the one to do first. This counts techniques the mapping reached, so it is a floor: a technique with no MITRE mitigation is not counted here at all, and the CVEs still need patching either way. The last column is MITRE's own wording for this control against that technique, trimmed of its citation markers and cut to its opening so the table stays a list rather than an essay. attack.mitre.org carries it in full.

panel.title: How an attacker would use this here

search.query: | `riskability_attack_patterns_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)` | join type=left cve_id [| `riskability_reachability_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)` | stats max(reach_rank) AS peak_reach BY cve_id ] | eval reach = case(peak_reach>=3,"answers any address",peak_reach>=2,"answers one address",peak_reach>=1,"loopback only",peak_reach>=0,"no listening port",1=1,"not assessed") | stats dc(cve_id) AS cves, values(reach) AS reach_seen, max(peak_reach) AS rk_sort, values(technique) AS techniques BY capec, capec_name, capec_abstraction, capec_severity, capec_likelihood, prerequisites, first_step | eval reach = case(rk_sort>=3,"answers any address",rk_sort>=2,"answers one address",rk_sort>=1,"loopback only",rk_sort>=0,"no listening port",1=1,"not assessed") | sort 50000 - rk_sort, - cves | head 60 | table reach, capec, capec_name, cves, capec_abstraction, capec_severity, capec_likelihood, prerequisites, first_step | rename reach AS "Reachable here", capec AS "CAPEC", capec_name AS "Attack pattern", cves AS "CVEs", capec_abstraction AS "Abstraction", capec_severity AS "MITRE rating", capec_likelihood AS "MITRE likelihood", prerequisites AS "Attacker needs", first_step AS "First move"

viz.option: No open finding maps to a CAPEC attack pattern in this scope.

div.b: Observed on the left, MITRE's generic rating on the right.
div.span: "Reachable here" is measured on your fleet: whether a copy of the vulnerable package answers the network. "MITRE rating" and "MITRE likelihood" are CAPEC's generic rating for the pattern, not a measurement of your host, and the two are kept apart on purpose so a high generic rating on something unreachable never outranks a reachable finding. The rows are sorted by reach first. "Attacker needs" and "First move" are CAPEC's own words for the entry requirement and the opening step.
